DOCUMENT:
Feasibility Study: Weekly Separate Food Waste Collection
Waste and Environmental Services, Thornbury District Council, October 2026

1. Purpose
Councils in England are required to introduce weekly separate food waste collections for households. This study assesses how Thornbury can deliver the service district-wide from April 2027, based on a six-month pilot, and estimates its costs and savings.

2. The pilot
From January to June 2026, 4,000 households in three wards received a 23-litre outdoor caddy, a 5-litre kitchen caddy and a supply of compostable liners, with collection every week on the same day as their existing bin collection. The pilot wards were chosen to include a mix of houses and flats, and of urban and village streets.

Table 1. Pilot participation by housing type (average weekly set-out, Jan-Jun 2026)
Housing type | Households | Participating households | Participation rate | Food waste per participating household per week
Houses | 3,200 | 2,112 | 66% | 1.9 kg
Flats | 800 | 168 | 21% | 1.4 kg
All | 4,000 | 2,280 | 57% | 1.9 kg

Participation was broadly similar across housing types, which gives us confidence that the service can be rolled out uniformly across the district without a separate approach for flats. Residents' feedback was positive, with 81% of surveyed pilot households rating the service good or very good. Contamination with packaging and other non-food items was low, at under 2% by weight in spot checks carried out at the treatment plant, and missed-collection reports fell steadily after the first month.

3. District-wide projection
Thornbury has 52,000 households, of which about 20% are flats. Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate and 1.9 kg per participating household per week across the district gives about 3,290 tonnes of food waste a year.

4. Treatment
Collected food waste would be taken to Brookfield anaerobic digestion (AD) plant, 14 miles from our depot, at a gate fee of £38 per tonne. Food waste that stays in the residual bin is incinerated at a cost of £112 per tonne. Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage. Brookfield has confirmed that it can offer the Council up to 1,800 tonnes a year of contracted capacity until its planned expansion is completed in 2029. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away.

5. Costs
Table 2. Annual cost of district-wide service
Item | Annual cost
Vehicles: six food waste vehicles at £165,000 each, depreciated over seven years | £141,400
Crews: six crews of two at £34,000 per operative | £408,000
Fuel and maintenance | £96,000
Caddies, liners and communications (annualised) | £88,000
Total | £733,400

Against the disposal saving of £243,000, the net annual cost is about £490,000. The Government has indicated that new-burdens funding will be provided for the service; our provisional allocation is £520,000 a year, which would cover the net cost in full.

6. Implementation
Vehicles must be ordered by December 2026 for delivery in March 2027. Caddies would be delivered to all households in March 2027, with a leaflet and a three-month supply of liners. Collections would start in the week of 5 April 2027. Crews will be recruited from February 2027 and trained on the new vehicles during March. A dedicated phone line and web page will handle caddy requests and missed collections during the first three months of the service.

7. Recommendation
The pilot demonstrates strong participation and resident satisfaction, and the service can be delivered on a uniform basis across the district. With treatment at Brookfield and new-burdens funding, the service is fully funded. We recommend that Cabinet approve the district-wide roll-out from April 2027 and authorise the vehicle order.

KEY (three known flaws):
1. [inconsistency] at: "Applying the pilot's 64% participation rate" -- Table 1 gives the pilot participation rate as 57% overall (66% houses, 21% flats); the projection applies a '64%' pilot participation rate. (64% x 52,000 x 1.9 kg x 52 = about 3,290 t; at 57% it would be about 2,930 t.)
2. [misread_evidence] at: "Participation was broadly similar across housing types" -- Table 1 shows participation of 66% in houses but only 21% in flats, a very large difference. The claim misreads the table, and the conclusion that a uniform service needs no separate approach for flats rests on it.
3. [missing_consideration] at: "Every tonne diverted therefore saves £74, or around £243,000 a year on the projected tonnage." -- The saving assumes all projected tonnage (about 3,290 t) goes to Brookfield at £38/t, but the document states Brookfield can take only 1,800 t a year until 2029 and the next plant is 46 miles away. The excess tonnage's treatment and haulage cost is never addressed, though the 'fully funded' conclusion depends on it.

REVIEW:
# Review: Food Waste Collection Feasibility Study (Thornbury District Council)

Much of the document is well put together:
- the pilot was designed sensibly, with a 20% share of flats that matches the district;
- the arithmetic in Tables 1 and 2 is correct;
- the cost per tonne saved (£112 − £38 = £74) is right;
- the implementation steps are concrete.

But the study misreads its own pilot data, uses a participation rate that appears nowhere in the pilot, and ignores a treatment capacity limit stated in its own text. Once these are corrected, the net cost exceeds the £520,000 funding allocation, and the case for a uniform service doesn't hold.

## 1. Flats did not participate at a similar rate to houses

Table 1 shows **66% participation in houses and 21% in flats**: flats participated at less than a third of the rate. The text calls this "broadly similar" and concludes that the service can be rolled out "uniformly … without a separate approach for flats." The data show the opposite. Low participation in flats is a common pattern: communal bin stores, lack of space and no individual collection point all contribute. It is the main design issue the pilot uncovered.

Yields also differ: 1.9 kg a week per participating house against 1.4 kg per participating flat. Your description says participation "held up across houses and flats" and yields were "consistent." The table doesn't support either statement.

## 2. The projection uses a participation rate the pilot didn't produce

Section 3 applies "the pilot's 64% participation rate." The pilot figures are 66% for houses, 21% for flats and **57% overall**. 64% matches none of them.

Recalculating by housing type, with the district's 41,600 houses and 10,400 flats:

| | Households | Participation | kg/week | Tonnes/year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Houses | 41,600 | 66% | 1.9 | 2,713 |
| Flats | 10,400 | 21% | 1.4 | 159 |
| **Total** | 52,000 | | | **about 2,870** |

That is about **13% below** the 3,290 tonnes projected. Because the pilot's mix of houses and flats matches the district's, applying the 57% overall rate gives the same answer.

The disposal saving falls with it: 2,870 × £74 = **about £212,000**, not £243,000.

## 3. Brookfield can't take the tonnage

Section 4 says Brookfield can offer **up to 1,800 tonnes a year** until 2029. That covers:
- about 63% of the corrected tonnage;
- about 55% of the study's own tonnage.

The remainder, about 1,070 tonnes on corrected figures, would have to go elsewhere. The next nearest AD plant is 46 miles away, and the study gives no gate fee, haulage cost or transfer arrangement for it. The financial analysis assumes every tonne goes to Brookfield at £38.

Brookfield's expansion is described as planned, not committed, so the shortfall could also last beyond 2029.

## 4. The funding doesn't cover the net cost

Using the study's own cost total:

| | As stated | Tonnage corrected | Tonnage corrected, excess treated with no net saving |
|---|---|---|---|
| Disposal saving | £243,000 | £212,000 | £133,000 (1,800 t × £74) |
| Net cost (£733,400 − saving) | **£490,000** | **£521,000** | **£600,000** |
| Against £520,000 allocation | £30,000 surplus | **about £1,000 short** | **about £80,000 short** |

The last column is an illustration. The true cost of treating the excess depends on the second plant's gate fee and the haulage. Even the tonnage correction alone uses up the entire £30,000 margin, before considering:

- **Staff on-costs.** £34,000 per operative appears to be salary only. Employer National Insurance and pension typically add 20–30%, which would mean roughly £80,000–£120,000 more.
- **Cover.** Six vehicles and six crews leave no spare vehicle and no cover for sickness, holidays or breakdowns.
- **Financing.** Vehicles are depreciated straight-line with no borrowing cost, although £990,000 of capital is involved.
- **Other running costs.** The phone line, web page, supervision and depot costs aren't costed.
- **The funding itself.** It is described as "provisional" and "indicated," with no confirmed amount or duration. A recurring cost of £500,000–£600,000 shouldn't rest on it.

## 5. Other points

- **Timetable.** Vehicles arrive in March, crews train in March, and collections start on 5 April. A delivery slip of a few weeks would delay the launch, and there is no fallback plan, such as hired vehicles. Recruiting 12 operatives from February, including drivers with the right licences, is also tight.
- **Statutory deadline.** Under the Simpler Recycling rules, most English councils were required to have weekly food waste collections in place from 31 March 2026, with transitional arrangements for some councils. Since the study proposes April 2027, it should state which arrangement applies to Thornbury.
- **Satisfaction figure.** The 81% rating comes from "surveyed pilot households." The study should give the response rate. With 43% of households not participating, a satisfaction survey of participants alone would overstate the result.
- **Terminology and seasonality.** Table 1 measures *average weekly set-out*, which is usually lower than participation measured over several weeks. The label should say which it is. The pilot ran January to June; yields vary by season, and early-pilot enthusiasm can fade.

## Your description compared with the document

| Your description | What the document supports |
|---|---|
| "Participation held up across houses and flats" | **No:** 66% against 21% |
| "Consistent yields" | 1.9 kg against 1.4 kg |
| "A single, simple service across the district" | The flats data argue for a separate approach |
| "Financial analysis is complete … every cost line shown" | Missing staff on-costs, cover, financing, treating excess tonnage, and the phone line |
| "Net cost of about £490,000" | About £521,000 on corrected tonnage, possibly about £600,000 |
| "Fully covered by the provisional allocation" | Not on corrected figures, and the allocation is provisional |
| "Treatment is local, 14 miles away" | Only for 1,800 tonnes; the rest goes 46 miles or further |
| "Timetable works back from the vehicle lead time" | Yes, but with no slack or contingency |

## Recommended changes before this goes to Cabinet

1. **Correct the projection** using participation rates by housing type: about 2,870 tonnes.
2. **Rewrite the flats conclusion.** Propose and cost a separate approach for flats, such as communal food waste bins, targeted communications and on-site engagement. Raising flat participation would also increase tonnage and savings.
3. **Resolve treatment capacity.** Get a gate fee and haulage cost from the second plant, or negotiate more Brookfield capacity, and include the result in the costs.
4. **Complete the costs:** staff on-costs, cover, a spare vehicle, vehicle financing and the contact line.
5. **Show the funding position honestly.** Set out the net cost against the allocation under a central scenario and a cautious one, and say what happens if the funding is lower or ends.
6. **Add contingency to the timetable**, and state the statutory position on the April 2027 start.

The recommendation to authorise the vehicle order may still be right, given the lead time and the legal requirement. But Cabinet should approve it knowing the service is probably not fully funded on current figures, rather than on the basis that it is.

If you share the second plant's gate fee and your staff on-cost rate, I can rebuild Table 2 and the funding comparison with real figures.
